# Deep Structural Models: Replicating the Sequential Search Transformer {#sec-deep-structural} @sec-structural-models argued that a structural parameter earns its keep by being invariant to the policy the analyst wants to study. @sec-ai-ml argued that a deep network earns its keep by extracting signal from data too rich for a hand-specified functional form. For two decades these two arguments ran on separate tracks. The structural modeler wrote down a small parametric utility and defended its identification. The machine learner fit a large flexible predictor and defended its out-of-sample loss. Each could point at the other's weakness. The structural model was too rigid to use a consumer's full behavioral history. The deep model produced no object that survived a change in the firm's policy. This chapter works through a paper that refuses the choice. @song2026sst propose the *sequential search transformer* (SST), which embeds the optimal sequential search problem of @weitzman1979optimal inside a transformer and trains the whole object end to end. The economics supplies the decision rule that maps latent quantities into observed clicks and purchases. The network supplies the map from a consumer's cross-session history into those latent quantities. Neither component is a wrapper around the other. The search model's reservation-utility equation is a differentiable layer through which gradients flow into the network's weights. The network's output is the economic primitive that the search model requires. The chapter is a replication, so it is organized as one. @sec-dss-paper states what the paper claims. @sec-dss-theory develops the search theory and implements its central object, the reservation utility, as code. @sec-dss-architecture assembles the architecture. @sec-dss-identification asks what can be recovered from search and purchase data when part of the model is a neural network. @sec-dss-likelihood and @sec-dss-estimation build the differentiable likelihood and confront the estimation problem it creates. @sec-dss-dgp through @sec-dss-ablation run the replication on a simulated clickstream whose primitives we know. @sec-dss-policy-rank through @sec-dss-policy-cost run the policy experiments. @sec-dss-limits separates what replicated from what did not, and @sec-dss-template extracts the template, because the reason to study this paper closely is that its architecture generalizes well beyond search. A note on what a replication of this kind can be. The paper's empirical section uses proprietary clickstream data from a U.S. e-commerce site, which is not available. A replication that cannot touch the data has two honest options. It can restate the model and stop, which teaches little. Or it can rebuild the model from the specification, generate data from a known process, and ask whether the method does what the paper says it does. We take the second route throughout. Every number in this chapter comes from code in this chapter, run against a data generating process whose true parameters are printed alongside the estimates. Where our results diverge from the paper's reported pattern, @sec-dss-limits says so. The code in this chapter is base R with no package dependencies, and a full execution takes roughly ten minutes, most of it in the three estimation runs of @sec-dss-prediction and the Monte Carlo of @sec-dss-montecarlo. ## The Paper and Its Claim {#sec-dss-paper} The abstract of @song2026sst makes four claims. It is worth separating them, because they are supported by different kinds of evidence and they replicate to different degrees. **Claim 1, architecture.** Deep learning and sequential search theory can be unified into a single end-to-end trainable model. This is a constructive claim. It is established by exhibiting the architecture, which we do in @sec-dss-architecture, and by showing that the resulting objective is differentiable in every parameter, which we verify numerically in @sec-dss-likelihood. **Claim 2, generalization of the search model.** Unlike existing sequential search models, SST models behavior *across* sessions and resolves utility uncertainty *sequentially* within a session. The first is about where the pre-search expected utility comes from. Classical implementations take it as a linear index in observed attributes, estimated within a session [@kim2010online; @ursu2018rankings; @ursu2025framework]. SST takes it as the output of an attention block over the consumer's past behavior, so preferences are dynamic and person-specific. The second is about what happens after a click. In the classical model, inspecting item $j$ resolves $j$'s match value and nothing else. In SST, the revealed match value of an inspected item updates beliefs about items that resemble it, so the reservation utilities of the remaining alternatives move as search proceeds. **Claim 3, identification.** All parameters are identified under the proposed framework. @sec-dss-identification takes this apart. The honest version of the claim is narrower than it sounds. The narrowing is instructive for anyone building a deep structural model. **Claim 4, performance and policy.** SST beats state-of-the-art deep learning and structural benchmarks at predicting searches and purchases. Its policy experiments improve recommendations and new-product promotion. This is the claim a replication can test most directly, and the one where our results are mixed in a way worth reporting. The intellectual position is worth naming, since it is now a recognizable genre. @farrell2021deep gave the inference theory for deep networks used as flexible first-stage components. @wei2024neural used networks as *estimators* of structural parameters, training a network to invert the mapping from data to parameters. @lu2026journeys used a transformer to model customer journeys. SST sits at a different point. The network here is none of those. It is the part of the economic model that the analyst previously had to guess. ## Sequential Search Theory {#sec-dss-theory} ### The consumer's problem A consumer faces $J$ alternatives. Alternative $j$ delivers utility $$ u_{j} = \delta_{j} + \varepsilon_{j}, $$ {#eq-dss-util} where $\delta_{j}$ is known before inspection and $\varepsilon_{j} \sim F$ is a match value revealed only by inspecting the item. Inspection is costly, at $c_{j} > 0$. The consumer may stop at any point and take the best alternative inspected so far, or take an outside option whose utility is normalized to zero. This is Pandora's box. @weitzman1979optimal shows the optimal policy is an index rule. Define the *reservation utility* $z_{j}$ as the value that makes the consumer indifferent between inspecting $j$ and stopping: $$ c_{j} \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[\max\left(u_{j} - z_{j},\, 0\right)\right] \;=\; \int_{z_{j}}^{\infty} (u - z_{j})\, dF_{j}(u). $$ {#eq-dss-resv} The optimal policy then has three parts. *Selection.* Inspect alternatives in descending order of $z_{j}$. *Stopping.* Stop when the best realized utility so far, including the outside option, exceeds the highest reservation utility among the alternatives not yet inspected. *Choice.* Take the inspected alternative with the highest realized utility, provided it beats the outside option. Three features of this rule drive everything that follows. First, the ordering of search is governed by $z$, while the final choice is governed by $u$. These are different objects. A consumer can rationally inspect an item first and buy a different one. Second, search costs enter *only* through $z$, so they are identified from stopping behavior and not from choice. Third, $z_j$ is a deterministic, monotone function of $\delta_j$ and $c_j$, which is exactly what makes the rule differentiable and therefore trainable. ### The reservation-utility layer With $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, write $z_{j} = \delta_{j} + m_{j}$. Then @eq-dss-resv reduces to a one-dimensional equation in $m_j$ alone, $$ \psi(m_{j}) \;\equiv\; \phi(m_{j}) - m_{j}\bigl(1 - \Phi(m_{j})\bigr) \;=\; c_{j}, $$ {#eq-dss-psi} where $\phi$ and $\Phi$ are the standard normal density and distribution function. $\psi$ is strictly decreasing, with $\psi(m) \to \infty$ as $m \to -\infty$ and $\psi(m) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$, so @eq-dss-psi has a unique root for any $c_j > 0$. Its derivative is unusually clean: $$ \psi'(m) \;=\; -\bigl(1 - \Phi(m)\bigr) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\partial m_{j}}{\partial c_{j}} \;=\; \frac{-1}{1 - \Phi(m_{j})}. $$ {#eq-dss-dmdc} @eq-dss-dmdc is the hinge of the whole architecture. It says the map from search cost to reservation cutoff has an exact, cheap derivative, so the economics can sit inside a computational graph as an ordinary layer. Everything downstream of it receives gradients. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # The Weitzman layer. psi() is the expected gain from inspecting an item whose # reservation cutoff is m; resv_m() inverts it; dm_dc() is the exact derivative # used in backpropagation. psi_fun <- function(m) dnorm(m) - m * pnorm(m, lower.tail = FALSE) resv_m <- function(cc) { # solve psi(m) = c, vectorised bisection lo <- rep(-40, length(cc)); hi <- rep(40, length(cc)) for (it in 1:80) { mid <- (lo + hi) / 2 gt <- psi_fun(mid) > cc # psi decreasing: root lies to the right lo <- ifelse(gt, mid, lo) hi <- ifelse(gt, hi, mid) } (lo + hi) / 2 } dm_dc <- function(m) -1 / pnorm(m, lower.tail = FALSE) # The inversion is exact to machine precision. cc <- c(0.002, 0.02, 0.2) cat("search cost :", cc, "\n") #> search cost : 0.002 0.02 0.2 cat("reservation cutoff :", round(resv_m(cc), 4), "\n") #> reservation cutoff : 2.5007 1.6631 0.4929 cat("psi(m) recovers c :", round(psi_fun(resv_m(cc)), 6), "\n") #> psi(m) recovers c : 0.002 0.02 0.2 ``` ::: The shape of this map explains a recurring finding in the empirical search literature, that estimated search costs are fragile even when search *behavior* is pinned down precisely. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2, 1)) cg <- exp(seq(log(1e-3), log(1), length.out = 300)) plot(cg, resv_m(cg), type = "l", lwd = 2, log = "x", xlab = "search cost c (log scale)", ylab = expression(m == psi^-1 * (c)), main = "Reservation cutoff") plot(cg, abs(dm_dc(resv_m(cg))), type = "l", lwd = 2, log = "xy", xlab = "search cost c (log scale)", ylab = expression(group("|", partialdiff * m / partialdiff * c, "|")), main = "Sensitivity") par(op) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The reservation-utility map. Left: the cutoff m as a function of search cost. Right: its derivative. At low search costs the map is nearly flat in m and extremely steep in c, so behaviour identifies the cutoff far more sharply than it identifies the cost that generated it.](29a-deep-structural-search_files/figure-html/fig-dss-resv-1.png){#fig-dss-resv fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ### What the classical model leaves unspecified Empirical implementations of this model set $\delta_{j} = x_{j}'\beta$ and $c_{j} = \exp(w_{j}'\gamma)$, with $x$ the attributes visible before a click and $w$ typically containing the item's position on the page [@kim2010online; @ursu2018rankings; @chen2017refinement; @honka2017simultaneous]. The linear index is a modeling convenience, and it carries two costs. It cannot use a consumer's history, because history is a variable-length sequence and $x_{j}'\beta$ takes a fixed-length vector. And it holds $\delta_{j}$ fixed within a session, so inspecting one item teaches the consumer nothing about any other. SST replaces the index with a network and relaxes both restrictions. The theory above is untouched. ## From Theory to Architecture {#sec-dss-architecture} The SST has three blocks. A cross-session encoder turns a consumer's history into a preference state. A within-session block lets resolved uncertainty spill onto un-inspected items. The Weitzman layer turns the resulting quantities into reservation utilities, which drive the likelihood. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-dss-arch %%| fig-cap: "The sequential search transformer. The left branch is deep learning, the right branch is economics, and they meet at the pre-search index and the search cost. Gradients flow back through the Weitzman layer into every network weight." flowchart TB H["Cross-session history:
items the consumer engaged with,
with recency"] --> ATT["Self-attention block
query, keys, values"] ATT --> HS["Preference state h(i,t)"] X["Displayed item attributes"] --> EMB["Item embedding e(i,j)"] EMB --> DELTA HS --> DELTA["Pre-search index
delta = alpha'x + e'h + spillover"] EMB --> SPILL["Within-session attention
over inspected items"] SPILL --> DELTA POS["Slot on the page"] --> COST["Search cost
c = exp(gamma0 + gamma1 * slot)"] COST --> WZ["Weitzman layer
m = psi inverse of c"] DELTA --> Z["Reservation utility
z = delta + m"] WZ --> Z Z --> LIK["Smoothed likelihood of the
observed click order, stopping
point and purchase"] DELTA --> LIK ``` ### Cross-session preference Let $\mathcal{H}_{it}$ be the items consumer $i$ engaged with before session $t$, ordered from most to least recent, with recency $g_{i\ell}$. Each item maps to an embedding through a shared linear map of its attributes, $e = W_e x$. Attention over the history produces the preference state, $$ a_{i\ell} = \frac{\exp\!\bigl( w_q' W_k e_{i\ell} / \sqrt{d} + \rho\, g_{i\ell} \bigr)} {\sum_{\ell'} \exp\!\bigl( w_q' W_k e_{i\ell'} / \sqrt{d} + \rho\, g_{i\ell'} \bigr)}, \qquad \tilde h_{it} = \sum_{\ell} a_{i\ell}\, W_v e_{i\ell}, $$ {#eq-dss-attn} followed by a residual feed-forward block, $h_{it} = \tilde h_{it} + W_2\,\mathrm{relu}(W_1 \tilde h_{it})$. The recency term $\rho$ is worth keeping explicit. It lets the model learn *how fast tastes drift*, a quantity the classical model has no slot for. Building the embedding from attributes, and not from an item identifier, is a design choice with a large payoff later. An item the model has never seen still has an embedding, so the architecture extends to products with no history. This is what makes the new-product experiment in @sec-dss-policy-newprod possible. ### The pre-search index and within-session learning For item $j$ displayed in session $t$, after $r-1$ inspections, $$ \delta_{ijt}^{(r)} \;=\; \underbrace{\alpha' x_{ijt}}_{\text{attributes}} \;+\; \underbrace{e_{ijt}' h_{it}}_{\text{fit to this consumer}} \;+\; \underbrace{\lambda \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}_{r-1}} A_{jk}\, \varepsilon_{k}}_{\text{resolved uncertainty}}, $$ {#eq-dss-delta} where $\mathcal{S}_{r-1}$ is the set already inspected and $A_{jk}$ is attention over inspected items, $A_{jk} \propto \exp(e_j'e_k/\sqrt{d})$ with $A_{jj}=0$. The third term is the paper's sequential resolution of uncertainty. A consumer who opens an item and finds it better than expected revises upward the items that resemble it. Setting $\lambda = 0$ recovers the classical model exactly, which makes $\lambda$ a testable restriction. One caveat belongs here and not in a footnote. Weitzman's index rule is optimal when match values are independent across alternatives. Once inspecting $k$ is informative about $j$, the exactly optimal policy is a harder dynamic program and the index rule becomes a one-step-ahead approximation. We follow the paper in applying the index rule to updated beliefs. The approximation is standard in this literature. Its cost is that $\lambda$ should be read as a behavioral parameter of a boundedly rational searcher. ### Search cost Search cost is specified as $c_{ijt} = \exp(\gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \cdot \mathrm{slot}_{jt})$, with slot the item's position on the page. Position is excluded from @eq-dss-delta. This exclusion is the identifying restriction that the empirical search literature has relied on since @kim2010online, and it is an assumption about the world, that where an item sits changes how hard it is to inspect without changing how much the consumer enjoys owning it. @ursu2018rankings tests it with exogenous ranking variation. In a replication we impose it by construction, and @sec-dss-identification shows what breaks without it. ## Identification {#sec-dss-identification} The paper states that all parameters are identified. A deep structural model needs this claim stated carefully, because two quite different objects are in play. The *structural functions* are $\delta(\cdot)$ and $c(\cdot)$, the maps from observables to the pre-search index and the search cost. The *network weights* are the parameters of a particular representation of those functions. Only the first is identified in any useful sense. That is enough. ### Normalizations Two normalizations are required and neither is testable. The scale is fixed by $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon) = 1$, because utility is ordinal and the data contain only comparisons. The location is fixed by setting the outside option's utility to zero. A third restriction does real work. The researcher-unobserved component of the pre-search index, $\eta_{ijt} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\eta^2)$, is known to the consumer before inspecting and unknown to the analyst. Without it the model predicts a deterministic search order, which the data reject immediately. ### What the data say Write the observed session as a triple: the ordered set of inspected items, the point at which search stopped, and the purchase. Each of the three margins speaks to a different part of the model. **Lemma 1 (choice identifies index differences).** The purchase is the arg-max of $u_j = \delta_j + \eta_j + \varepsilon_j$ over the inspected set and the outside option. The inspected set is endogenous, because the same $\eta_j$ that raises $\delta_j$ also raises $z_j$ and makes item $j$ more likely to be opened. The model handles that selection explicitly. The search rule is a known function of $z$, so the joint probability that *this set was inspected and this item was bought* is a computable function of $(\delta, m, \sigma_\eta)$. Holding $m$ fixed, variation in which items are displayed across sessions moves that probability only through the differences $\delta_j - \delta_k$, which identifies $\delta(\cdot)$ up to location. This is the discrete-choice argument on a varying choice set [@train2009discrete], with the consideration stage modeled as part of the likelihood. **Lemma 2 (order identifies the ranking of reservation utilities).** The selection rule inspects in descending $z$. The probability that $j$ is inspected before $k$ is $\Pr(z_j > z_k)$, which depends on the parameters only through $(\delta_j - \delta_k) + (m_j - m_k)$ and $\sigma_\eta$. Given $\delta(\cdot)$ from Lemma 1, the observed order identifies $m_j - m_k$. **Lemma 3 (stopping identifies the level).** Search stops when the best realized utility exceeds the largest remaining $z$. The distribution of the *number* of inspections therefore identifies the level of $m$ relative to the utility distribution, which is pinned down by the normalizations. **Proposition.** Under the two normalizations, a known $F$, and the exclusion of slot position from @eq-dss-delta, the functions $\delta(\cdot)$ and $c(\cdot)$ are identified from the joint distribution of inspected sets, search order, stopping points and purchases. $c$ follows from $m$ because $\psi$ in @eq-dss-psi is strictly monotone, so $c = \psi(m)$ is a bijection. The proof sketch is the three lemmas in sequence: choice fixes $\delta$, order fixes differences in $m$ given $\delta$, stopping fixes the level of $m$, and the Weitzman map converts $m$ into $c$. @ursu2025framework give the argument for the classical model in far more detail, including the role of exclusion restrictions and the conditions under which search costs are separately identified from preferences. The deep model changes none of the logic. It changes only the class of functions that $\delta(\cdot)$ is allowed to live in. ### What is not identified, and why it does not matter The network weights are not identified. Rotating the embedding space and applying the inverse rotation to $W_v$ leaves $e'h$ unchanged, so whole manifolds of weights generate the same $\delta$. Nothing that a firm or a researcher wants to know depends on which point in that manifold the optimizer lands on. This is the practical content of the distinction above. A deep structural model should report the structural functions, the elasticities they imply, and the counterfactuals they generate, and it should not report a table of network weights with standard errors. Two failure modes do matter. Without the position exclusion, a shift in $\delta$ and an offsetting shift in $m$ leave the search order unchanged, so preferences and search costs cannot be separated from ordering data alone. And because $\psi$ is nearly flat at small $c$ (@fig-dss-resv), the level of the *cost* is estimated far less precisely than the level of the *cutoff*. @sec-dss-montecarlo shows both effects in numbers. ## The Likelihood and Why It Must Be Differentiable {#sec-dss-likelihood} ### The event Given draws of $\eta$ and $\varepsilon$, the policy is deterministic, so the observed session is an event in the space of those draws. Let items be inspected in order $s_1, \dots, s_n$, let $\mathcal{U}_r$ be the set not yet inspected at step $r$, and let $u^{*}$ be the realized utility of the purchased item, or zero when nothing was bought. The event is the intersection of four families of inequalities. $$ \begin{aligned} \text{(a) selection} \quad & z_{s_r}^{(r)} \ge z_{k}^{(r)} && \forall\, k \in \mathcal{U}_r \setminus \{s_r\},\ r = 1,\dots,n,\\ \text{(b) continuation} \quad & z_{s_r}^{(r)} > u_{s_t} \ \text{ and } \ z_{s_r}^{(r)} > 0 && \forall\, t < r,\ r = 1,\dots,n,\\ \text{(c) stopping} \quad & u^{*} \ge z_{k}^{(n+1)} && \forall\, k \in \mathcal{U}_{n+1},\\ \text{(d) choice} \quad & u^{*} \ge u_{s_t} && \forall\, t \le n . \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-dss-event} Writing the event this way, as a product of pairwise comparisons, matters. The stopping rule compares a maximum against a maximum, which is not differentiable term by term. Conditions (c) and (d) together replace it: the choice condition already identifies which inspected item attains the maximum, so the stopping comparison can be written against that single item. ### Smoothing The likelihood of a session is the probability of @eq-dss-event, a high-dimensional orthant probability with no closed form. The standard estimator simulates draws and counts the fraction satisfying the inequalities, which is a step function of the parameters and cannot be differentiated. Replacing each indicator with a logistic kernel at temperature $\tau$ gives the smoothed simulated likelihood of @mcfadden1989msm, $$ \hat \ell_i = \log \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} \prod_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_i} \sigma\!\left( \frac{d_q^{(s)}}{\tau} \right), $$ {#eq-dss-smooth} where $d_q$ runs over the differences in @eq-dss-event. This is the step that makes the model *end-to-end trainable*. It is also the step that introduces the estimation problem of @sec-dss-estimation, so it belongs in the specification section of a paper and not in a footnote about computation. ### Implementation The functions below implement the network forward pass, @eq-dss-smooth, and its exact gradient. The code is longer than the rest of the chapter combined, and it is folded by default. Two design points are worth seeing. Draws are held fixed across optimization steps, which turns a stochastic objective into a deterministic one. And the gradient is analytic throughout, including through the Weitzman layer via @eq-dss-dmdc, so no finite differencing is needed anywhere. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Parameter packing. A "spec" switches the deep components on and off, which is # how the ablations in this chapter are built: use_hist = FALSE and # use_spill = FALSE reproduces the classical sequential search model exactly. sst_spec <- function(d_emb = 6L, d_ff = 12L, use_hist = TRUE, use_spill = TRUE, n_lin = 3L, n_att = 4L) { sh <- list(alpha = c(n_lin, 1L)) if (use_hist || use_spill) sh$W_e <- c(d_emb, n_att) if (use_hist) { sh$w_q <- c(d_emb, 1L); sh$W_k <- c(d_emb, d_emb); sh$W_v <- c(d_emb, d_emb) sh$rho <- c(1L, 1L); sh$W1 <- c(d_ff, d_emb); sh$W2 <- c(d_emb, d_ff) } sh$gam <- c(2L, 1L) if (use_spill) sh$lam <- c(1L, 1L) sh$lsig <- c(1L, 1L) list(shapes = sh, d_emb = d_emb, d_ff = d_ff, use_hist = use_hist, use_spill = use_spill) } unpack <- function(v, spec) { out <- list(); k <- 0L for (nm in names(spec$shapes)) { s <- spec$shapes[[nm]]; n <- s[1] * s[2] out[[nm]] <- matrix(v[k + seq_len(n)], s[1], s[2]); k <- k + n } out } pack <- function(p, spec) unlist(lapply(names(spec$shapes), function(nm) as.vector(p[[nm]]))) n_par <- function(spec) sum(vapply(spec$shapes, function(s) as.numeric(s[1]) * s[2], 0)) init_par <- function(spec, seed = 11) { set.seed(seed) p <- list() for (nm in names(spec$shapes)) { s <- spec$shapes[[nm]] p[[nm]] <- matrix(rnorm(s[1] * s[2], 0, 0.15), s[1], s[2]) } p$alpha[1] <- -1.5 p$gam <- matrix(c(-4, 0.1), 2, 1) if (!is.null(p$lam)) p$lam[1] <- 0.1 p$lsig[1] <- log(0.7) pack(p, spec) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Data preparation. Sessions index rows; simulation draws are stacked so that # every array is a matrix with (session, draw) rows and item columns. prep <- function(d, S = 32L, seed = 99) { N <- d$N; J <- d$J; L <- d$L Xd2 <- matrix(d$Xd, N * J, 4) Xlin <- cbind(1, Xd2[, 1], Xd2[, 2]) # intercept, price, rating Xh2 <- d$cat_x[as.vector(d$hist_item), ] gapv <- as.vector(d$hist_gap) posv <- as.vector(d$pos) Rmax <- max(d$nsearch) sb <- vector("list", Rmax + 1L) # already inspected before step r sb[[1]] <- matrix(FALSE, N, J) if (Rmax >= 1) for (r in seq_len(Rmax)) { m <- sb[[r]]; act <- d$nsearch >= r if (any(act)) m[cbind(which(act), d$ord[act, r])] <- TRUE sb[[r + 1L]] <- m } rbuy <- integer(N) for (i in seq_len(N)) if (d$buy[i] > 0) rbuy[i] <- match(d$buy[i], d$ord[i, seq_len(d$nsearch[i])]) set.seed(seed) list(N = N, J = J, L = L, S = S, Rmax = Rmax, Xd2 = Xd2, Xlin = Xlin, Xh2 = Xh2, gapv = gapv, posv = posv, ord = d$ord, nsearch = d$nsearch, buy = d$buy, rbuy = rbuy, sb = sb, Zeta = matrix(rnorm(N * S * J), N * S, J), Zeps = matrix(rnorm(N * S * J), N * S, J), rowi = rep(seq_len(N), S), idx = seq_len(N * S)) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Encoder: attention over the consumer's history produces the preference state. enc_forward <- function(p, P, spec) { N <- P$N; L <- P$L; d <- spec$d_emb cache <- list(); Ed <- NULL if (spec$use_hist || spec$use_spill) Ed <- P$Xd2 %*% t(p$W_e) if (spec$use_hist) { Eh <- P$Xh2 %*% t(p$W_e) K <- Eh %*% t(p$W_k) scv <- as.vector(K %*% p$w_q) / sqrt(d) + p$rho[1] * P$gapv scM <- matrix(scv, N, L); scM <- scM - apply(scM, 1, max) Ex <- exp(scM); att <- Ex / rowSums(Ex) V <- Eh %*% t(p$W_v) hraw <- matrix(0, N, d) for (k in seq_len(d)) hraw[, k] <- rowSums(att * matrix(V[, k], N, L)) pre <- hraw %*% t(p$W1); ffh <- pmax(pre, 0) h <- hraw + ffh %*% t(p$W2) cache <- list(Eh = Eh, K = K, att = att, V = V, hraw = hraw, pre = pre, ffh = ffh) } else { h <- matrix(0, N, d) } list(Ed = Ed, h = h, cache = cache) } # Full forward pass: pre-search index, search cost, Weitzman cutoff, and the # within-session attention weights that carry resolved uncertainty. net_forward <- function(p, P, spec) { N <- P$N; J <- P$J; d <- spec$d_emb en <- enc_forward(p, P, spec) Ed <- en$Ed; h <- en$h; cache <- en$cache; Aw <- NULL dbar <- as.vector(P$Xlin %*% p$alpha) if (spec$use_hist) { hrep <- h[rep(seq_len(N), J), , drop = FALSE] dbar <- dbar + rowSums(Ed * hrep) cache$hrep <- hrep } dbar <- matrix(dbar, N, J) cc <- exp(p$gam[1] + p$gam[2] * P$posv) cc <- pmin(pmax(cc, 1e-5), 20) mres <- matrix(resv_m(cc), N, J) if (spec$use_spill) { M1 <- array(Ed, c(N, J, d)) jj <- rep(seq_len(J), each = J); kk <- rep(seq_len(J), times = J) Scf <- matrix(0, N, J * J) for (k in seq_len(d)) Scf <- Scf + M1[, jj, k] * M1[, kk, k] Sc <- aperm(array(Scf / sqrt(d), c(N, J, J)), c(1, 3, 2)) for (j in seq_len(J)) Sc[, j, j] <- -Inf mx <- Sc[, , 1];
