A wrong gradient produces a model that trains to something plausible and false. The check is central differences on every coordinate. The check is run in @sec-dss-dgp, once the data generating process is in place, so that it exercises the same code path the estimates use. ## Estimation: Smoothed Simulated Maximum Likelihood {#sec-dss-estimation} The smoothing temperature $\tau$ in @eq-dss-smooth is usually presented as a nuisance to be taken as small as possible. That advice is wrong. Getting it wrong silently destroys the estimates. Two biases move in opposite directions as $\tau$ falls. The first is *smoothing bias*. A logistic kernel at temperature $\tau$ behaves like an extra logistic disturbance of scale $\tau$ added to every comparison, so a large $\tau$ inflates the apparent noise in the model and, under a fixed scale normalization, inflates every utility coefficient. This bias vanishes as $\tau \to 0$, which is the source of the usual advice. The second is *simulation bias*, and it grows as $\tau$ falls. @eq-dss-smooth takes the log of a simulated average. As the kernel sharpens, each draw's contribution approaches zero or one, the simulated average becomes the fraction of draws satisfying a rare event. The log of that average then acquires a downward bias whose size grows as the true probability falls. The optimizer responds by moving to parameters that make every draw moderately compatible with the data, which shrinks every utility coefficient toward zero. This is the failure mode that looks like a converged model and reports estimates that are wrong by a factor of two. The second bias admits a diagnostic that needs no knowledge of the truth. Evaluate the objective at a fixed parameter vector across a grid of $S$. Simulation bias is what makes the objective move as draws are added, so the size of that movement measures it. The first bias is invisible to any such diagnostic, because it is a property of the estimand and not of the simulation. The operating point therefore has to be chosen by Monte Carlo against a known truth. @sec-dss-montecarlo does exactly that. The practical rule that emerges is to take $\tau$ as small as the draw budget allows, verify with the diagnostic that simulation bias is small at that pair, and confirm the choice by recovery on simulated data. The optimizer is Adam with a decaying step size, run on the full sample with fixed draws. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_model <- function(objfun, v0, steps = 300, lr0 = 0.06, lr_decay = 0.1) { v <- v0; m <- rep(0, length(v)); s <- rep(0, length(v)); path <- numeric(steps) for (t in seq_len(steps)) { lr <- lr0 * lr_decay^((t - 1) / max(steps - 1, 1)) o <- objfun(v); gr <- o$grad gn <- sqrt(sum(gr^2)); if (gn > 5) gr <- gr * 5 / gn # gradient clipping m <- 0.9 * m + 0.1 * gr; s <- 0.999 * s + 0.001 * gr^2 v <- v - lr * (m / (1 - 0.9^t)) / (sqrt(s / (1 - 0.999^t)) + 1e-8) path[t] <- o$nll } list(par = v, nll = path[steps], path = path) } ``` ::: ## A Simulated Clickstream {#sec-dss-dgp} The data generating process below is the SST's own structure run forward. Consumers have a two-dimensional taste vector that drifts across periods as an AR(1). In each period they engage with items aligned to their current taste, which becomes the history the encoder sees at the next session. In a session, eight items are displayed in slots, the consumer follows Weitzman's policy with position-dependent search costs, and inspecting an item shifts beliefs about items with similar style attributes. Three features keep this a fair test. The taste vector is latent, so the encoder must infer it from behavior and will do so imperfectly. Taste drifts, so a model that weights all history equally is misspecified. And position enters search cost only, so the exclusion restriction of @sec-dss-identification holds by construction and a model that ignores it can be shown to fail. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} make_catalog <- function(M) cbind(price = rnorm(M), rating = rnorm(M), st1 = rnorm(M), st2 = rnorm(M)) # Similarity weights that carry resolved uncertainty between displayed items. sim_weights <- function(Xs, temp = 0.7) { S <- (Xs %*% t(Xs)) / temp diag(S) <- -Inf E <- exp(S - apply(S, 1, max)) E / rowSums(E) } sim_data <- function(n_users = 700, n_sess = 2, J = 8, L = 10, M = 400, alpha = c(int = -2.3, price = -0.55, rating = 0.50), gam0 = log(0.004), gam1 = 0.65, sig_eta = 0.8, lambda = 1.0, sim_temp = 0.7, rho_ar = 0.75, sig_tau = 0.9, kappa = 1.4, n_burn = 2L, seed = 1) { set.seed(seed) cat_x <- make_catalog(M) N <- n_users * n_sess b_per <- L %/% n_burn hist_item <- matrix(0L, N, L); hist_gap <- matrix(0, N, L) disp_item <- matrix(0L, N, J) user_id <- integer(N); sess_id <- integer(N); tau_now <- matrix(0, N, 2) row <- 0L for (u in seq_len(n_users)) { tau <- rnorm(2, 0, sig_tau) buf <- integer(0) for (t in seq_len(n_sess + n_burn)) { tau <- rho_ar * tau + sqrt(1 - rho_ar^2) * rnorm(2, 0, sig_tau) if (t > n_burn) { row <- row + 1L user_id[row] <- u; sess_id[row] <- t - n_burn hist_item[row, ] <- buf[seq_len(L)] # strictly past behaviour hist_gap[row, ] <- (seq_len(L) - 1) / L disp_item[row, ] <- sample.int(M, J) tau_now[row, ] <- tau } pref <- kappa * (cat_x[, "st1"] * tau[1] + cat_x[, "st2"] * tau[2]) buf <- c(sample.int(M, b_per, replace = FALSE, prob = exp(pref - max(pref))), buf) } } pos <- matrix(rep(seq_len(J) - 1, each = N), N, J) mres <- matrix(resv_m(as.vector(exp(gam0 + gam1 * pos))), N, J) Xd <- array(0, c(N, J, 4)) for (k in 1:4) Xd[, , k] <- matrix(cat_x[disp_item, k], N, J) dbar <- alpha["int"] + alpha["price"] * Xd[, , 1] + alpha["rating"] * Xd[, , 2] + tau_now[, 1] * Xd[, , 3] + tau_now[, 2] * Xd[, , 4] eta <- matrix(rnorm(N * J, 0, sig_eta), N, J) eps <- matrix(rnorm(N * J), N, J) ord <- matrix(0L, N, J); nsearch <- integer(N); buy <- integer(N) for (i in seq_len(N)) { A <- sim_weights(cbind(Xd[i, , 3], Xd[i, , 4]), sim_temp) d0 <- dbar[i, ] + eta[i, ] spill <- rep(0, J); unsearched <- rep(TRUE, J) best <- 0; best_j <- 0L; r <- 0L repeat { if (!any(unsearched)) break z <- d0 + lambda * spill + mres[i, ] z[!unsearched] <- -Inf jstar <- which.max(z) if (best >= z[jstar]) break # stopping rule r <- r + 1L; ord[i, r] <- jstar # selection rule u_j <- d0[jstar] + lambda * spill[jstar] + eps[i, jstar] if (u_j > best) { best <- u_j; best_j <- jstar } unsearched[jstar] <- FALSE spill <- spill + A[, jstar] * eps[i, jstar] # resolved uncertainty } nsearch[i] <- r buy[i] <- best_j # 0 means no purchase } list(N = N, J = J, L = L, M = M, cat_x = cat_x, disp_item = disp_item, hist_item = hist_item, hist_gap = hist_gap, Xd = Xd, pos = pos, ord = ord, nsearch = nsearch, buy = buy, user_id = user_id, sess_id = sess_id, tau_now = tau_now, truth = list(alpha = alpha, gam0 = gam0, gam1 = gam1, sig_eta = sig_eta, lambda = lambda, sim_temp = sim_temp)) } # The true structural primitives, available only because this is a simulation. true_primitives <- function(d) { N <- d$N; J <- d$J; tr <- d$truth dbar <- tr$alpha["int"] + tr$alpha["price"] * d$Xd[, , 1] + tr$alpha["rating"] * d$Xd[, , 2] + d$tau_now[, 1] * d$Xd[, , 3] + d$tau_now[, 2] * d$Xd[, , 4] mres <- matrix(resv_m(as.vector(exp(tr$gam0 + tr$gam1 * d$pos))), N, J) Aw <- array(0, c(N, J, J)) for (i in seq_len(N)) Aw[i, , ] <- sim_weights(cbind(d$Xd[i, , 3], d$Xd[i, , 4]), tr$sim_temp) list(dbar = dbar, mres = mres, Aw = Aw, lam = tr$lambda, sig = tr$sig_eta) } click_matrix <- function(d) { Y <- matrix(0, d$N, d$J) for (i in seq_len(d$N)) if (d$nsearch[i] > 0) Y[i, d$ord[i, seq_len(d$nsearch[i])]] <- 1 Y } subset_d <- function(d, idx) { d$Xd <- d$Xd[idx, , , drop = FALSE] for (nm in c("hist_item", "hist_gap", "disp_item", "pos", "ord", "tau_now")) d[[nm]] <- d[[nm]][idx, , drop = FALSE] for (nm in c("nsearch", "buy", "user_id", "sess_id")) d[[nm]] <- d[[nm]][idx] d$N <- length(idx) d } ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-dss-descriptives .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Descriptive statistics of the simulated clickstream. The position gradient in click rates is generated entirely by the search-cost function, because position is excluded from utility.'} ```{.r .cell-code} dat <- sim_data(n_users = 700, n_sess = 2, seed = 20) Yobs <- click_matrix(dat) cat("sessions :", dat$N, "\n") #> sessions : 1400 cat("consumers :", length(unique(dat$user_id)), "\n") #> consumers : 700 cat("mean items inspected :", round(mean(dat$nsearch), 3), "\n") #> mean items inspected : 1.7 cat("sessions with no click :", round(mean(dat$nsearch == 0), 3), "\n") #> sessions with no click : 0.066 cat("purchase rate :", round(mean(dat$buy > 0), 3), "\n") #> purchase rate : 0.484 cat("bought item was 1st click:", round(mean(dat$buy[dat$buy > 0] == dat$ord[dat$buy > 0, 1]), 3), "\n\n") #> bought item was 1st click: 0.728 cat("click rate by slot :", round(colMeans(Yobs), 3), "\n") #> click rate by slot : 0.422 0.324 0.273 0.234 0.174 0.139 0.085 0.05 cat("inspections per session :", table(dat$nsearch), "\n") #> inspections per session : 93 546 509 198 48 6 ``` ::: Two descriptive facts already discipline the model. The click rate falls steeply across slots even though slot is irrelevant to utility, which is the signature of a search cost. And in more than a quarter of purchases the consumer bought something other than the first item inspected, which is the signature of a stopping rule: a consumer who could see all match values would never open a second item. ### The gradient check ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dsm <- subset_d(dat, 1:40) Psm <- prep(dsm, S = 6, seed = 1) variants <- list("full SST" = sst_spec(4, 6, TRUE, TRUE), "cross-session only" = sst_spec(4, 6, TRUE, FALSE), "classical SSM" = sst_spec(4, 6, FALSE, FALSE)) for (nm in names(variants)) { sp <- variants[[nm]] set.seed(3); v <- init_par(sp) + rnorm(n_par(sp), 0, 0.05) an <- sst_obj(v, Psm, sp)$grad fd <- vapply(seq_along(v), function(k) { e <- rep(0, length(v)); e[k] <- 1e-5 (sst_obj(v + e, Psm, sp, grad = FALSE)$nll - sst_obj(v - e, Psm, sp, grad = FALSE)$nll) / (2e-5) }, 0) cat(sprintf("%-20s %3d parameters max relative error %.2e\n", nm, n_par(sp), max(abs(an - fd) / (abs(an) + 1e-4)))) } #> full SST 108 parameters max relative error 2.06e-07 #> cross-session only 107 parameters max relative error 1.61e-06 #> classical SSM 6 parameters max relative error 8.72e-11 ``` ::: Every analytic gradient agrees with central differences to seven digits, in all three variants. The backward pass through the Weitzman layer, the within-session attention and the recursive belief update is correct. ## Monte Carlo: Does the Estimator Recover the Truth? {#sec-dss-montecarlo} Before asking whether the deep model beats its benchmarks, ask whether the estimator works at all. The cleanest test shuts off the features that put the truth outside the estimated model class. Setting the taste variance to zero and $\lambda$ to zero makes the data generating process exactly the classical sequential search model, whose parameters the classical specification can represent exactly. Anything other than recovery is then an estimator failure. ### The temperature diagnostic First the diagnostic of @sec-dss-estimation. Evaluate the objective at a fixed parameter vector across $\tau$ and $S$, and look for flatness in $S$. ::: {#tbl-dss-tau-diag .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Simulation bias in the smoothed log-likelihood. Entries are the negative log-likelihood per session at the true parameter vector. Reading down a column shows how much of the objective at a given draw count is simulation bias, because that bias is what the extra draws remove.'} ```{.r .cell-code} dmc <- sim_data(n_users = 300, n_sess = 2, sig_tau = 0, lambda = 0, seed = 11) spec_c <- sst_spec(6, 12, use_hist = FALSE, use_spill = FALSE) v_true <- pack(list(alpha = matrix(c(dmc$truth$alpha), 3, 1), gam = matrix(c(dmc$truth$gam0, dmc$truth$gam1), 2, 1), lsig = matrix(log(dmc$truth$sig_eta), 1, 1)), spec_c) taus <- c(0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45); Sg <- c(20, 40, 80, 160) diag_tab <- outer(Sg, taus, Vectorize(function(S, tt) sst_obj(v_true, prep(dmc, S = S, seed = 7), spec_c, tsm = tt, grad = FALSE)$nll)) dimnames(diag_tab) <- list(paste0("S=", Sg), paste0("tau=", taus)) round(diag_tab, 3) #> tau=0.15 tau=0.25 tau=0.35 tau=0.45 #> S=20 6.498 5.619 5.491 5.612 #> S=40 5.358 4.992 5.069 5.297 #> S=80 4.832 4.704 4.866 5.134 #> S=160 4.347 4.423 4.666 4.976 ``` ::: Read the table down each column. At $\tau = 0.15$ the objective moves by more than two log points between 20 and 160 draws, so most of what the optimizer sees at 20 draws is simulation bias. At $\tau = 0.45$ the same range of draws moves it by a fraction of that. The diagnostic orders the columns correctly and bounds one of the two biases. It cannot pick the operating point on its own, because it is monotone in $\tau$ and would always recommend more smoothing. The next table supplies the missing half. ### Parameter recovery ::: {#tbl-dss-mc .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Monte Carlo recovery when the truth lies inside the estimated model class. Each row is a separate estimation run on the same 600 sessions. Low temperatures shrink every utility coefficient toward zero, exactly as the simulation-bias argument predicts.'} ```{.r .cell-code} Pmc <- prep(dmc, S = 40, seed = 7) cfgs <- c(0.15, 0.30, 0.45) mc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(cfgs), function(i) { f <- fit_model(function(v) sst_obj(v, Pmc, spec_c, tsm = cfgs[i]), init_par(spec_c), steps = 250) p <- unpack(f$par, spec_c) data.frame(tau = cfgs[i], intercept = p$alpha[1], price = p$alpha[2], rating = p$alpha[3], log_cost = p$gam[1], slot = p$gam[2], sigma_eta = exp(p$lsig[1])) })) truth_row <- data.frame(tau = NA, intercept = dmc$truth$alpha[1], price = dmc$truth$alpha[2], rating = dmc$truth$alpha[3], log_cost = dmc$truth$gam0, slot = dmc$truth$gam1, sigma_eta = dmc$truth$sig_eta) round(rbind(mc, truth = truth_row), 3) #> tau intercept price rating log_cost slot sigma_eta #> 1 0.15 -1.527 -0.338 0.313 -3.625 0.341 0.481 #> 2 0.30 -2.209 -0.591 0.558 -5.158 0.649 0.882 #> 3 0.45 -2.625 -0.776 0.738 -5.918 0.829 1.162 #> truth NA -2.300 -0.550 0.500 -5.521 0.650 0.800 ``` ::: The bias is U-shaped in $\tau$, exactly as the two-bias argument predicts. At $\tau = 0.15$ with 40 draws every coefficient has collapsed toward zero, which is simulation bias. At $\tau = 0.45$ every coefficient overshoots, which is smoothing bias. At $\tau = 0.30$ the estimates land on the truth, including the slot coefficient of the search-cost function. This is the single most important practical lesson in the chapter for anyone implementing a differentiable structural likelihood. Neither bias announces itself in a fit statistic, and the two can cancel at one sample size but not at another. The interior optimum is invisible unless the estimator is run against a known truth. The estimates in the rest of the chapter use $\tau = 0.30$ with 64 draws, a larger draw budget than this table uses, because the deep specifications carry more parameters and need more of the simulation bias removed at the same temperature. One caveat that @sec-dss-identification anticipated. The slot coefficient and the cutoff $m$ are recovered sharply. The cost *level* is recovered with much less precision, because @fig-dss-resv is nearly flat in $m$ at small $c$, so a large relative error in the cost maps into a small error in behavior. Search costs reported in currency units should be read with that in mind. ## Replication: Predictive Performance {#sec-dss-prediction} ### The benchmarks The paper compares SST against state-of-the-art deep learning and structural models. A replication has to choose benchmarks. The choice decides how informative the comparison is. We use three. The **classical sequential search model** is the SST with the deep components switched off, so $\delta = \alpha'x$ and $\lambda = 0$. This is the structural benchmark, in the spirit of @kim2010online and @ursu2018rankings. The **cross-session ablation** keeps the history encoder and sets $\lambda = 0$. It isolates what the transformer contributes separately from what the within-session learning contributes. The **deep benchmark** is deliberately strong. It shares the SST's encoder exactly, including the attention over history and the residual block, and replaces the search theory with two prediction heads: an independent Bernoulli head for clicks and a softmax head over the displayed items plus the outside option for purchase. It is trained directly on the cross-entropy of the outcomes being predicted. This is a harder benchmark than a generic sequence recommender, because it has identical representational capacity and an objective aligned with the evaluation metric. If structure buys anything, it has to buy it against this. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} bb_spec <- function(d_emb = 6L, d_ff = 12L, n_lin = 3L, n_att = 4L) { sh <- list(W_e = c(d_emb, n_att), w_q = c(d_emb, 1L), W_k = c(d_emb, d_emb), W_v = c(d_emb, d_emb), rho = c(1L, 1L), W1 = c(d_ff, d_emb), W2 = c(d_emb, d_ff), a_c = c(n_lin, 1L), g_c = c(1L, 1L), W_c = c(d_emb, d_emb), a_b = c(n_lin, 1L), g_b = c(1L, 1L), W_b = c(d_emb, d_emb)) list(shapes = sh, d_emb = d_emb, d_ff = d_ff, use_hist = TRUE, use_spill = FALSE) } bb_obj <- function(v, P, spec, ycl, grad = TRUE) { p <- unpack(v, spec); N <- P$N; J <- P$J; d <- spec$d_emb en <- enc_forward(p, P, spec); Ed <- en$Ed; h <- en$h hrep <- h[rep(seq_len(N), J), , drop = FALSE] Hcr <- (h %*% t(p$W_c))[rep(seq_len(N), J), , drop = FALSE] Hbr <- (h %*% t(p$W_b))[rep(seq_len(N), J), , drop = FALSE] sc <- as.vector(P$Xlin %*% p$a_c) + p$g_c[1] * P$posv + rowSums(Ed * Hcr) sb <- as.vector(P$Xlin %*% p$a_b) + p$g_b[1] * P$posv + rowSums(Ed * Hbr) yc <- as.vector(ycl) llc <- sum(yc * plogis(sc, log.p = TRUE) + (1 - yc) * plogis(-sc, log.p = TRUE)) sbM <- cbind(0, matrix(sb, N, J)) # column 1 is no purchase Eb <- exp(sbM - apply(sbM, 1, max)); pb <- Eb / rowSums(Eb) llb <- sum(log(pb[cbind(seq_len(N), P$buy + 1L)])) nll <- -(llc + llb) / N if (!grad) return(list(nll = nll, pclick = matrix(plogis(sc), N, J), pbuy = pb[, -1, drop = FALSE], pnobuy = pb[, 1])) gsc <- (plogis(sc) - yc) / N gsbM <- pb gsbM[cbind(seq_len(N), P$buy + 1L)] <- gsbM[cbind(seq_len(N), P$buy + 1L)] - 1 gsb <- as.vector(gsbM[, -1, drop = FALSE]) / N g <- list(a_c = matrix(crossprod(P$Xlin, gsc), nrow(p$a_c), 1), a_b = matrix(crossprod(P$Xlin, gsb), nrow(p$a_b), 1), g_c = matrix(sum(gsc * P$posv), 1, 1), g_b = matrix(sum(gsb * P$posv), 1, 1), W_c = crossprod(gsc * Ed, hrep), W_b = crossprod(gsb * Ed, hrep)) Qc <- matrix(0, N, d); Qb <- matrix(0, N, d) for (k in seq_len(d)) { Qc[, k] <- rowSums(matrix(gsc * Ed[, k], N, J)) Qb[, k] <- rowSums(matrix(gsb * Ed[, k], N, J)) } g <- c(g, enc_backward(Qc %*% p$W_c + Qb %*% p$W_b, gsc * Hcr + gsb * Hbr, p, P, en, spec)) list(nll = nll, grad = pack(g[names(spec$shapes)], spec)) } ``` ::: ### Turning a structural model into a predictor A structural model does not emit click and purchase probabilities directly. It emits primitives. The probabilities come from running the estimated policy forward, which is the same operation that later produces counterfactuals. Using one routine for both is the point: a model that can predict this way can also answer questions about worlds it has not seen. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Forward simulation of the optimal sequential-search policy. Works identically # on estimated primitives and on the true ones. sim_policy <- function(dbar, mres, Aw, lam, sig, ndraw = 500, seed = 4242) { N <- nrow(dbar); J <- ncol(dbar); NS <- N * ndraw set.seed(seed) rep_i <- rep(seq_len(N), ndraw); idx <- seq_len(NS) D0 <- dbar[rep_i, , drop = FALSE] + sig * matrix(rnorm(NS * J), NS, J) Eps <- matrix(rnorm(NS * J), NS, J) Mr <- mres[rep_i, , drop = FALSE] spill <- matrix(0, NS, J); searched <- matrix(FALSE, NS, J) clicks <- matrix(0, NS, J); best <- numeric(NS); bestj <- integer(NS) active <- rep(TRUE, NS); nsr <- integer(NS) for (r in seq_len(J)) { if (!any(active)) break z <- D0 + Mr + lam * spill z[searched] <- -Inf jst <- max.col(z, ties.method = "first") go <- active & (z[cbind(idx, jst)] > best) # stopping rule if (!any(go)) break sel <- cbind(idx, jst) clicks[sel] <- clicks[sel] + go nsr <- nsr + go u <- (D0 + lam * spill + Eps)[sel] upd <- go & (u > best) best[upd] <- u[upd]; bestj[upd] <- jst[upd] searched[sel] <- searched[sel] | go if (lam != 0) { Acols <- matrix(0, NS, J) for (j in seq_len(J)) Acols[, j] <- Aw[cbind(rep_i, j, jst)] spill <- spill + go * Acols * Eps[sel] } active <- go } pclick <- matrix(0, N, J); pbuy <- matrix(0, N, J) for (j in seq_len(J)) { pclick[, j] <- rowMeans(matrix(clicks[, j], N, ndraw)) pbuy[, j] <- rowMeans(matrix(bestj == j, N, ndraw)) } list(pclick = pclick, pbuy = pbuy, pnobuy = 1 - rowSums(pbuy), en = rowMeans(matrix(nsr, N, ndraw))) } auc <- function(score, y) { r <- rank(score); n1 <- sum(y == 1); n0 <- sum(y == 0) if (n1 == 0 || n0 == 0) return(NA_real_) (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0) } eval_pred <- function(pclick, pbuy, pnobuy, d, eps = 1e-6) { Y <- click_matrix(d) pc <- pmin(pmax(pclick, eps), 1 - eps) pmat <- cbind(pmax(pnobuy, eps), pmax(pbuy, eps)); pmat <- pmat / rowSums(pmat) c(ll_click = mean(Y * log(pc) + (1 - Y) * log(1 - pc)), auc_click = auc(as.vector(pclick), as.vector(Y)), ll_buy = mean(log(pmat[cbind(seq_len(d$N), d$buy + 1L)])), hit_buy = mean(max.col(pmat, ties.method = "first") - 1L == d$buy), rmse_n = sqrt(mean((rowSums(pclick) - d$nsearch)^2))) } mres_from_rank <- function(rankmat, gam0, gam1) matrix(resv_m(as.vector(exp(gam0 + gam1 * (rankmat - 1)))), nrow(rankmat), ncol(rankmat)) rank_by <- function(score) t(apply(score, 1, function(s) rank(-s, ties.method = "first"))) predict_layout <- function(par, spec, P, rankmat = NULL, ndraw = 500, seed = 4242) { p <- unpack(par, spec); fw <- net_forward(p, P, spec) mres <- if (is.null(rankmat)) fw$mres else mres_from_rank(rankmat, p$gam[1], p$gam[2]) Aw <- if (is.null(fw$Aw)) array(0, c(P$N, P$J, P$J)) else fw$Aw sim_policy(fw$dbar, mres, Aw, if (spec$use_spill) p$lam[1] else 0, exp(p$lsig[1]), ndraw = ndraw, seed = seed) } truth_layout <- function(d, rankmat = NULL, ndraw = 500, seed = 4242) { tp <- true_primitives(d) mres <- if (is.null(rankmat)) tp$mres else mres_from_rank(rankmat, d$truth$gam0, d$truth$gam1) sim_policy(tp$dbar, mres, tp$Aw, tp$lam, tp$sig, ndraw = ndraw, seed = seed) } bb_layout <- function(par, spec, P, rankmat = NULL) { if (!is.null(rankmat)) P$posv <- as.vector(rankmat - 1) bb_obj(par, P, spec, matrix(0, P$N, P$J), grad = FALSE) } ``` ::: ### Estimation Consumers are split into estimation and holdout groups, so no holdout consumer's history is seen during training. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dtr <- subset_d(dat, which(dat$user_id <= 400)) dte <- subset_d(dat, which(dat$user_id > 400)) Ptr <- prep(dtr, S = 64, seed = 7) Pte <- prep(dte, S = 64, seed = 8) specs <- list(SSM = sst_spec(6, 12, use_hist = FALSE, use_spill = FALSE), SSTh = sst_spec(6, 12, use_hist = TRUE, use_spill = FALSE), SST = sst_spec(6, 12, use_hist = TRUE, use_spill = TRUE)) fits <- lapply(specs, function(sp) fit_model(function(v) sst_obj(v, Ptr, sp, tsm = 0.30), init_par(sp), steps = 260)) bsp <- bb_spec(6, 12) bfit <- fit_model(function(v) bb_obj(v, Ptr, bsp, click_matrix(dtr)), init_par(bsp), steps = 400, lr0 = 0.05) cat("training sessions:", dtr$N, " holdout sessions:", dte$N, "\n") #> training sessions: 800 holdout sessions: 600 for (nm in names(specs)) cat(sprintf("%-5s %4d parameters\n", nm, n_par(specs[[nm]]))) #> SSM 6 parameters #> SSTh 253 parameters #> SST 254 parameters cat(sprintf("%-5s %4d parameters\n", "DL", n_par(bsp))) #> DL 327 parameters ``` ::: ### Held-out performance ::: {#tbl-dss-pred .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Held-out predictive performance. Click and purchase entries are mean log-likelihoods, so larger is better; rmse_n is the error in predicted inspections per session, so smaller is better. Oracle evaluates the true primitives and bounds what any estimator could achieve at this sample size.'} ```{.r .cell-code} pred <- lapply(names(specs), function(nm) { s <- predict_layout(fits[[nm]]$par, specs[[nm]], Pte) eval_pred(s$pclick, s$pbuy, s$pnobuy, dte) }) names(pred) <- c("classical SSM", "SST cross-session", "SST full") bo <- bb_obj(bfit$par, Pte, bsp, click_matrix(dte), grad = FALSE) pred[["deep benchmark"]] <- eval_pred(bo$pclick, bo$pbuy, bo$pnobuy, dte) spo <- truth_layout(dte) pred[["oracle"]] <- eval_pred(spo$pclick, spo$pbuy, spo$pnobuy, dte) round(do.call(rbind, pred), 4) #> ll_click auc_click ll_buy hit_buy rmse_n #> classical SSM -0.4443 0.7765 -1.5975 0.5133 0.9384 #> SST cross-session -0.4098 0.8293 -1.4455 0.5133 0.9194 #> SST full -0.3982 0.8350 -1.4132 0.5183 0.9090 #> deep benchmark -0.4005 0.8339 -1.4246 0.5100 0.9483 #> oracle -0.2812 0.9247 -1.0195 0.6117 0.8311 ``` ::: The ablation is monotone. Adding the cross-session encoder to the classical search model improves four of the five metrics and leaves purchase hit rate unchanged. Adding within-session resolution of uncertainty improves all five. That is claim 2 of @sec-dss-paper, and it replicates. Against the deep benchmark the full SST is ahead on all five metrics, which is claim 4. The margins are small on click and purchase log-likelihood and larger on search depth. That pattern is what the two objectives imply. The benchmark optimizes the cross-entropy of the outcomes it is scored on, which is why it stays close on those two columns despite having no theory of how a session unfolds. It has no mechanism that generates a search depth at all, so its predicted inspection count is a sum of independent click probabilities. The `rmse_n` column shows the cost of that. One caution before this is read as a clean win. The margin on purchase log-likelihood is small and it is not robust in our design. @sec-dss-limits reports a variant with a larger estimation sample in which the benchmark overtakes SST on that one column while SST keeps its advantage everywhere else. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pc_ssm <- predict_layout(fits$SSM$par, specs$SSM, Pte)$pclick pc_sst <- predict_layout(fits$SST$par, specs$SST, Pte)$pclick Yte <- click_matrix(dte) op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2, 1)) plot(1:dte$J, colMeans(Yte), type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 0.5), xlab = "slot on the page", ylab = "click rate", main = "") lines(1:dte$J, colMeans(pc_ssm), type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2, lwd = 2) lines(1:dte$J, colMeans(pc_sst), type = "b", pch = 2, lty = 3, lwd = 2) legend("topright", c("observed", "classical SSM", "SST full"), pch = c(16, 1, 2), lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2, bty = "n") par(op) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Click rate by slot, observed and predicted. The classical model reproduces the aggregate position gradient because it has a search-cost function, but it cannot say which consumer clicks which item. The full SST matches both margins.](29a-deep-structural-search_files/figure-html/fig-dss-position-1.png){#fig-dss-position fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ## What the Deep Component Buys {#sec-dss-ablation} Predictive metrics compress a lot into one number. The structural estimates say more directly what the transformer is doing. ::: {#tbl-dss-params .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Estimated structural parameters against the truth. The deep specifications recover the search-cost function, which the classical model badly understates because it must absorb preference heterogeneity into the search process.'} ```{.r .cell-code} tp_te <- true_primitives(dte) par_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(specs), function(nm) { p <- unpack(fits[[nm]]$par, specs[[nm]]) fw <- net_forward(p, Pte, specs[[nm]]) data.frame(intercept = p$alpha[1], price = p$alpha[2], rating = p$alpha[3], log_cost = p$gam[1], slot = p$gam[2], lambda = if (is.null(p$lam)) 0 else p$lam[1], sigma_eta = exp(p$lsig[1]), cor_delta = cor(as.vector(fw$dbar), as.vector(tp_te$dbar)), sd_total = sqrt(var(as.vector(fw$dbar)) + exp(p$lsig[1])^2)) })) rownames(par_tab) <- c("classical SSM", "SST cross-session", "SST full") tr <- dat$truth par_tab <- rbind(par_tab, truth = data.frame(intercept = tr$alpha[1], price = tr$alpha[2], rating = tr$alpha[3], log_cost = tr$gam0, slot = tr$gam1, lambda = tr$lambda, sigma_eta = tr$sig_eta, cor_delta = 1, sd_total = sqrt(var(as.vector(tp_te$dbar)) + tr$sig_eta^2))) round(par_tab, 3) #> intercept price rating log_cost slot lambda sigma_eta #> classical SSM -1.717 -0.368 0.313 -4.223 0.493 0.00 1.061 #> SST cross-session -2.108 -0.395 0.404 -4.921 0.612 0.00 1.164 #> SST full -1.955 -0.366 0.383 -4.683 0.558 1.89 1.005 #> truth -2.300 -0.550 0.500 -5.521 0.650 1.00 0.800 #> cor_delta sd_total #> classical SSM 0.514 1.170 #> SST cross-session 0.714 1.539 #> SST full 0.725 1.349 #> truth 1.000 1.691 ``` ::: Four things in this table matter. **The classical model understates the position effect on search cost.** Its slot coefficient sits well below the truth, and its cost level is off by more than a log point. The mechanism is the one @sec-dss-identification described. Preference heterogeneity that the classical model cannot represent has to go somewhere. The only flexible margin left is the search process, so unexplained variation in which items get clicked is read as variation in the cost of clicking. This is a bias in a quantity firms act on. No fit statistic reveals it. **The deep specifications move the search-cost function toward the truth.** With the encoder in place the slot coefficient rises substantially and the cost level follows. The deep component is not decoration on the structural parameters. It is what makes them estimable. Both deep specifications still fall short of the truth at this sample size, so the correction is partial. **$\sigma_\eta$ sits above its nominal truth, which is correct behavior.** The truth value describes a world where the analyst knows the taste vector. The estimator does not know it, and recovers it only partially, so the residual belongs in the unobserved component. The column to read is `sd_total`, the implied dispersion of the full pre-search index. It rises toward the truth as the deep components are added, while staying below it at this sample size. The network's job is to move variance out of the unexplained bucket and into the explained one. The `cor_delta` column shows how far it gets. **$\lambda$ is over-estimated by roughly a factor of two. The raw coefficient is the wrong thing to read.** The within-session attention weights are learned, so they are not the true similarity weights. A learned weight profile that is more diffuse than the truth spreads the same information over more items, so $\lambda$ scales up to compensate. The coefficient is therefore not comparable across parameterizations. The comparable object is the behavior it implies: how much a consumer revises their expectation of the most similar remaining item after one click. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Expected belief revision about the most similar un-inspected item after the # first click, in units of the match-value standard deviation. p_sst <- unpack(fits$SST$par, specs$SST) fw_sst <- net_forward(p_sst, Pte, specs$SST) fc1 <- dte$ord[, 1] peak <- function(Aw) mean(vapply(seq_along(fc1), function(i) if (fc1[i] > 0) max(Aw[i, -fc1[i], fc1[i]]) else NA_real_, 0), na.rm = TRUE) cat("attention on the nearest item truth:", round(peak(tp_te$Aw), 3), " SST:", round(peak(fw_sst$Aw), 3), "\n") #> attention on the nearest item truth: 0.504 SST: 0.409 cat("implied revision per click truth:", round(tr$lambda * peak(tp_te$Aw), 3), " SST:", round(p_sst$lam[1] * peak(fw_sst$Aw), 3), "\n") #> implied revision per click truth: 0.504 SST: 0.773 ``` ::: The learned attention is flatter than the truth, so $\lambda$ absorbs the difference. The implied revision is over-stated by much less than the coefficient is, which is the general lesson for reporting deep structural estimates: report the behavior the parameters imply, because the parameters themselves are only defined relative to a representation the estimator chose. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} att_prof <- colMeans(enc_forward(p_sst, Pte, specs$SST)$cache$att) op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2, 1)) barplot(att_prof, names.arg = 1:length(att_prof), ylab = "mean attention weight", xlab = "history position (1 = most recent)") abline(h = 1 / length(att_prof), lty = 2) par(op) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Learned attention over the consumer's history, by recency. The encoder places more weight on recent behaviour, which is the correct response to a taste process that drifts. Nothing in the specification forced this; the weight profile is estimated.](29a-deep-structural-search_files/figure-html/fig-dss-attention-1.png){#fig-dss-attention fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ## Policy Experiment 1: Ranking {#sec-dss-policy-rank} The first policy question is the one every marketplace faces. Given a set of items and a set of slots, which item goes where? Under the model this is a well-posed problem. Slot determines search cost, search cost determines the reservation utility, and reservation utilities determine what gets inspected, so moving an item up the page raises the chance it is inspected and therefore the chance it is bought. Every candidate policy below is derived from an estimated model and then *evaluated under the true data generating process*, which is the luxury a simulation buys. The oracle policy ranks on the true pre-search index and bounds what is achievable. Revenue is the purchase probability weighted by a price of $40 + 10 \times$ the standardized price attribute. ::: {#tbl-dss-policy1 .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Ranking policies, evaluated under the true data generating process. Each policy is chosen by one model and scored by the truth.'} ```{.r .cell-code} rev_of <- function(pbuy, Xd, base = 40, slope = 10) rowSums(pbuy * (base + slope * Xd[, , 1])) set.seed(31) pbb <- unpack(bfit$par, bsp); enb <- enc_forward(pbb, Pte, bsp) Hbr <- (enb$h %*% t(pbb$W_b))[rep(seq_len(Pte$N), Pte$J), , drop = FALSE] score <- list( random = matrix(runif(dte$N * dte$J), dte$N, dte$J), `classical SSM` = net_forward(unpack(fits$SSM$par, specs$SSM), Pte, specs$SSM)$dbar, `deep benchmark` = matrix(as.vector(Pte$Xlin %*% pbb$a_b) + rowSums(enb$Ed * Hbr), Pte$N, Pte$J), `SST full` = fw_sst$dbar, oracle = tp_te$dbar) rk <- lapply(score, rank_by) pol1 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rk, function(R) { s <- truth_layout(dte, rankmat = R) c(P_buy = mean(rowSums(s$pbuy)), revenue = mean(rev_of(s$pbuy, dte$Xd)), inspections = mean(s$en)) })) pol1 <- cbind(pol1, `revenue gain %` = 100 * (pol1[, "revenue"] / pol1["random", "revenue"] - 1)) round(pol1, 4) #> P_buy revenue inspections revenue gain % #> random 0.5247 18.0651 1.6868 0.0000 #> classical SSM 0.5526 18.7370 1.9473 3.7195 #> deep benchmark 0.5552 19.0037 2.0002 5.1960 #> SST full 0.5550 18.9847 1.9968 5.0904 #> oracle 0.5636 19.4293 2.1023 7.5519 ``` ::: Personalized ranking is worth real money here. The size of the prize is set by how well a model recovers individual preferences. The classical search model, which has no way to personalize, captures part of the gain because it can still sort on price and rating. The SST and the deep benchmark capture most of it and are close to each other, which is the expected result: choosing a ranking requires only the *ordering* of preferences within a session. Both models learn that ordering from the same data through the same encoder. ### Choosing a policy is easier than forecasting one The comparison above understates the difference between the two approaches, because picking the best of five layouts is a much weaker requirement than saying what any of them will earn. A firm deciding whether a re-ranking project is worth doing needs the second. The table below asks each model to forecast revenue under each layout, and scores the forecast against the truth. ::: {#tbl-dss-policy-eval .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Forecast revenue under each layout, against the realised value. The deep benchmark has a position coefficient, so it produces a number, but the number comes from a reduced-form association estimated under the observed assignment and does not extrapolate.'} ```{.r .cell-code} fc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rk, function(R) c( realised = mean(rev_of(truth_layout(dte, rankmat = R)$pbuy, dte$Xd)), `SST full` = mean(rev_of(predict_layout(fits$SST$par, specs$SST, Pte, rankmat = R)$pbuy, dte$Xd)), `classical SSM` = mean(rev_of(predict_layout(fits$SSM$par, specs$SSM, Pte, rankmat = R)$pbuy, dte$Xd)), `deep benchmark` = mean(rev_of(bb_layout(bfit$par, bsp, Pte, rankmat = R)$pbuy, dte$Xd))))) round(fc, 3) #> realised SST full classical SSM deep benchmark #> random 18.065 17.690 19.535 16.760 #> classical SSM 18.737 18.511 20.103 17.410 #> deep benchmark 19.004 18.891 19.909 18.153 #> SST full 18.985 19.021 19.924 17.971 #> oracle 19.429 18.673 19.911 17.781 cat("\nmean absolute forecast error\n") #> #> mean absolute forecast error round(colMeans(abs(fc[, -1, drop = FALSE] - fc[, "realised"])), 3) #> SST full classical SSM deep benchmark #> 0.301 1.032 1.229 ``` ::: All three forecasts carry level error. The SST's is the smallest. The reason the structural forecast is better is not that its parameters are more accurate in some abstract sense. It is that a change in slot assignment enters the SST through the object that slot actually manipulates, the search cost, and propagates through a stopping rule that then determines purchases. The deep benchmark has a slot coefficient in a purchase softmax, which summarizes how purchases and slots covaried under the assignment it was trained on. That coefficient is a reduced form of the search process and it is not stable when the assignment changes. This is the Lucas critique in a recommender system. Read the level errors as a caution about the method too. An estimated structural model forecasting the value of its own preferred policy is evaluating that policy under its own beliefs. Those beliefs are over-confident about the part of preference the network explains. Reported counterfactual gains from a fitted structural model should be treated as upper bounds unless validated against held-out policy variation. ## Policy Experiment 2: New Product Promotion {#sec-dss-policy-newprod} A new product has attributes and no behavioral history. The firm can promote it to a fraction of visitors by placing it in the top slot, which pushes an incumbent off the page. Two things must be forecast to do this well. Which consumers will like the new item, and what the promotion costs in cannibalized sales of the item it displaces. This is where an item embedding built from attributes pays off. The encoder maps the new item's attributes into the same space as everything else, so the model has an opinion about it without ever having seen it chosen. ::: {#tbl-dss-policy2 .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='New-product targeting. The top 30% of consumers by each model\'s predicted adoption are shown the new item in the top slot, and outcomes are computed under the true data generating process including the cannibalization of the displaced item.'} ```{.r .cell-code} insert_new_product <- function(d, new_x) { J <- d$J; N <- d$N; d2 <- d d2$cat_x <- rbind(d$cat_x, new_x) d2$disp_item <- cbind(nrow(d2$cat_x), d$disp_item[, seq_len(J - 1), drop = FALSE]) Xd <- array(0, c(N, J, 4)) for (k in 1:4) Xd[, , k] <- matrix(d2$cat_x[d2$disp_item, k], N, J) d2$Xd <- Xd d2$ord <- matrix(0L, N, J); d2$nsearch <- integer(N); d2$buy <- integer(N) d2 } new_x <- matrix(c(-0.4, 1.0, 0.9, -0.7), 1, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("price", "rating", "st1", "st2"))) dnew <- insert_new_product(dte, new_x) Pnew <- prep(dnew, S = 8, seed = 9) targeting <- list( `SST full` = predict_layout(fits$SST$par, specs$SST, Pnew)$pbuy[, 1], `classical SSM` = predict_layout(fits$SSM$par, specs$SSM, Pnew)$pbuy[, 1], `deep benchmark` = bb_obj(bfit$par, Pnew, bsp, matrix(0, dnew$N, dnew$J), grad = FALSE)$pbuy[, 1]) truth_new <- truth_layout(dnew) targeting$oracle <- truth_new$pbuy[, 1] set.seed(5); targeting$random <- runif(dte$N) base_t <- truth_layout(dte) rev_base <- rev_of(base_t$pbuy, dte$Xd) rev_new <- rev_of(truth_new$pbuy, dnew$Xd) adopt <- truth_new$pbuy[, 1] k <- round(0.30 * dte$N) pol2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(targeting, function(sc) { tgt <- rep(FALSE, dte$N); tgt[order(sc, decreasing = TRUE)[1:k]] <- TRUE c(adoption_among_targeted = mean(adopt[tgt]), revenue = mean(ifelse(tgt, rev_new, rev_base)), gain_vs_no_promotion = mean(ifelse(tgt, rev_new, rev_base)) - mean(rev_base)) })) round(pol2, 4) #> adoption_among_targeted revenue gain_vs_no_promotion #> SST full 0.1810 18.8396 0.7607 #> classical SSM 0.1236 18.3910 0.3121 #> deep benchmark 0.1888 18.8945 0.8156 #> oracle 0.2415 19.2418 1.1630 #> random 0.0957 18.2788 0.1999 cat("\nrevenue with no promotion :", round(mean(rev_base), 3), "\n") #> #> revenue with no promotion : 18.079 cat("revenue promoting to all :", round(mean(rev_new), 3), "\n") #> revenue promoting to all : 19.094 ``` ::: Targeting on the model roughly doubles adoption relative to random targeting, and both the SST and the deep benchmark capture a similar share of the oracle's gain. The classical search model does much worse, because without a preference representation it can only say that the new item is good on average. A promotion policy that cannot distinguish between consumers is close to promoting at random. ## Policy Experiment 3: Lowering Search Costs {#sec-dss-policy-cost} The two experiments above rearrange things the benchmark model has a coefficient for. The third does not. Suppose the platform ships a quick-view feature that halves the cost of inspecting an item. Nothing about preferences changes, nothing about the assortment changes, and no coefficient in the deep benchmark corresponds to the intervention. The benchmark cannot answer. Its failure is structural: it has no object to perturb. The structural model has exactly one: $\gamma_0$ shifts by $\log 0.5$. ::: {#tbl-dss-policy3 .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Halving search costs. Changes are relative to the status quo under each model\'s own primitives. The deep benchmark is absent because the intervention has no representation in it.'} ```{.r .cell-code} qv <- log(0.5) m_qv_hat <- matrix(resv_m(as.vector(exp(p_sst$gam[1] + qv + p_sst$gam[2] * Pte$posv))), Pte$N, Pte$J) sst_qv <- sim_policy(fw_sst$dbar, m_qv_hat, fw_sst$Aw, p_sst$lam[1], exp(p_sst$lsig[1])) m_qv_true <- matrix(resv_m(as.vector(exp(tr$gam0 + qv + tr$gam1 * Pte$posv))), Pte$N, Pte$J) tru_qv <- sim_policy(tp_te$dbar, m_qv_true, tp_te$Aw, tp_te$lam, tp_te$sig) base_s <- predict_layout(fits$SST$par, specs$SST, Pte) pol3 <- rbind( truth = c(inspections = mean(tru_qv$en) - mean(base_t$en), P_buy = mean(rowSums(tru_qv$pbuy)) - mean(rowSums(base_t$pbuy)), revenue = mean(rev_of(tru_qv$pbuy, dte$Xd)) - mean(rev_of(base_t$pbuy, dte$Xd))), `SST full` = c(inspections = mean(sst_qv$en) - mean(base_s$en), P_buy = mean(rowSums(sst_qv$pbuy)) - mean(rowSums(base_s$pbuy)), revenue = mean(rev_of(sst_qv$pbuy, dte$Xd)) - mean(rev_of(base_s$pbuy, dte$Xd)))) round(pol3, 4) #> inspections P_buy revenue #> truth 0.3698 0.0250 0.9078 #> SST full 0.4501 0.0396 1.4746 ``` ::: The SST gets the direction and the rough magnitude of all three responses. It over-states the revenue gain, for the reason given in @sec-dss-policy-rank. As an input to a build-or-not decision on a quick-view feature, a forecast of this quality is worth having. No reduced-form alternative produces one at all. This is the clearest statement of what the structural half of a deep structural model buys. It is not accuracy on the training distribution. It is the existence of an answer off it. ## What Replicates and What Does Not {#sec-dss-limits} A replication is only useful if it is specific about its own limits. **Replicates.** The architecture works as described. The Weitzman equation is a differentiable layer with an exact derivative. Gradients reach every network weight, verified to seven digits in @sec-dss-dgp. The ablation in @sec-dss-prediction is monotone: cross-session attention improves on the classical model, and within-session resolution of uncertainty improves further. The deep component makes the structural parameters estimable, shown in @sec-dss-ablation, where the classical model mis-estimates the search-cost function because it must absorb preference heterogeneity into the search process. The policy experiments work. The gap between choosing a policy and forecasting its value in @sec-dss-policy-rank is where structure earns its keep. **Replicates with a caveat.** Identification. The functions $\delta(\cdot)$ and $c(\cdot)$ are identified under the normalizations and the position exclusion, which is what the paper's claim has to mean. The network weights are not identified and do not need to be. The cost *level* is weakly identified for the reason in @fig-dss-resv, so search costs reported in currency should carry that qualification. **Replicates, but fragile.** The predictive comparison against the deep benchmark. In the configuration reported in @sec-dss-prediction, 800 estimation sessions and 600 holdout sessions, the full SST is ahead on all five metrics. In a variant we also ran, with 960 estimation sessions and 440 holdout sessions, the benchmark overtakes SST on purchase log-likelihood by about 0.05 while SST keeps its advantage on click prediction, click AUC and search depth. The direction of that shift is what theory predicts, because a correctly specified structural model buys efficiency and the value of efficiency falls as data accumulate. A benchmark trained directly on purchase cross-entropy should also be hardest to beat on exactly that loss. We report it because a margin that flips with the split is not a margin to build a claim on. The robust part of claim 4 in our replication is the advantage on sequence-level quantities, where the benchmark has no mechanism at all, and the policy results below. **Does not separate.** Two of the three policy experiments. On ranking and on new-product targeting, the deep benchmark matches SST. Both experiments rearrange objects the benchmark has a coefficient for, and both require only that a model order preferences correctly within a session, which the shared encoder does equally well in either model. A replication that ran only those two experiments would conclude that the structural half of the model is unnecessary. The separation appears in the forecasting exercise of @sec-dss-policy-rank and, decisively, in @sec-dss-policy-cost. **Cannot be assessed.** Everything specific to the paper's data. Magnitudes of search costs in a real category, the shape of real cross-session preference dynamics, the size of the revenue gains on the firm's actual traffic, and whether the identifying exclusion holds on that site. A simulation can establish that a method recovers a truth. It cannot establish that a particular estimate describes the world. **Estimation caveats that generalize.** Two are worth carrying into any project of this kind. The smoothing temperature trades two biases against each other and has an interior optimum that depends on the draw budget and on the size of the model, so it must be calibrated by Monte Carlo, per @sec-dss-montecarlo. And a fitted structural model evaluating its own preferred policy is over-optimistic, so counterfactual gains should be reported as upper bounds unless they are validated against held-out policy variation. @sec-dss-policy-cost over-states the revenue gain from halving search costs by about sixty percent while getting the sign and the order of magnitude right, which is roughly the accuracy this class of exercise delivers at this sample size. ## Scaling Up {#sec-dss-scaling} Everything above is base R with hand-derived gradients, which is the right choice for a chapter whose purpose is to make the mechanism inspectable. It is the wrong choice for a project. At realistic scale, use automatic differentiation and mini-batching, and keep the structural layer exactly as it is written here. The sketch below is the same model in `torch`, which is the stable choice in R because it links to libtorch directly and needs no Python installation. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(torch) # The Weitzman layer. Only the inversion needs a custom derivative, and it is # available in closed form from @eq-dss-dmdc, so autograd handles everything else. resv_layer <- autograd_function( forward = function(ctx, cc) { m <- torch_tensor(resv_m(as.numeric(cc$cpu())))$view_as(cc) ctx$save_for_backward(m = m) m }, backward = function(ctx, grad_output) { m <- ctx$saved_variables$m # dm/dc = -1 / (1 - Phi(m)) list(cc = grad_output * (-1 / (1 - torch_special_ndtr(m)))) } ) sst_module <- nn_module( initialize = function(d_emb, d_ff, n_att, n_lin, n_head = 4) { self$emb <- nn_linear(n_att, d_emb, bias = FALSE) self$attn <- nn_multihead_attention(d_emb, n_head, batch_first = TRUE) self$ff <- nn_sequential(nn_linear(d_emb, d_ff), nn_relu(), nn_linear(d_ff, d_emb)) self$norm <- nn_layer_norm(d_emb) self$alpha <- nn_linear(n_lin, 1, bias = FALSE) self$gam <- nn_parameter(torch_tensor(c(-4, 0.1))) self$lam <- nn_parameter(torch_tensor(0.1)) self$lsig <- nn_parameter(torch_tensor(log(0.7))) }, forward = function(x_item, x_hist, mask_hist, slot) { e_h <- self$emb(x_hist) h <- self$attn(e_h[, 1:1, ], e_h, e_h, key_padding_mask = mask_hist)[[1]] h <- self$norm(h + self$ff(h)) e_j <- self$emb(x_item) list(dbar = self$alpha(x_item)$squeeze(-1) + torch_einsum("bjd,bod->bj", list(e_j, h)), m = resv_layer(torch_exp(self$gam[1] + self$gam[2] * slot)), e = e_j) } ) ``` ::: Three practical notes for that implementation. Mini-batch over sessions and keep the simulation draws fixed within a batch, so the objective a batch sees is deterministic. Anneal the smoothing temperature downward only while increasing the number of draws, guided by the diagnostic of @sec-dss-montecarlo. And carry the likelihood's inequality loop as a masked tensor operation over search steps, which is what the R code above does with matrices and is the only part that needs care to vectorize. ## Using This as a Model Paper {#sec-dss-template} The reason to study SST closely is that almost nothing in it is about search. Strip the application away and a template remains. It applies wherever a behavioral theory produces a decision rule and a firm holds rich individual-level data. **One.** Find the place where the economic model asks for a primitive the analyst cannot observe. In sequential search it is the pre-search expected utility. In a dynamic durable-goods model it is the expected flow utility. In a learning model it is the prior. Classical practice fills that slot with a linear index because it must, and the linear index is usually the least defended part of the model. **Two.** Put a network in that slot, and only in that slot. The economics stays untouched. The test of a deep structural model is whether the theory would still be recognizable if the network were replaced by a linear index, and whether that replacement nests as a restriction. Here it does, exactly, which is what makes the ablation in @sec-dss-prediction interpretable. **Three.** Make the decision rule differentiable, and prefer a rule whose derivative you can write down. @eq-dss-dmdc is the whole reason the SST trains. It exists because Weitzman's equation has a clean implicit derivative. When the rule is a maximum or an ordering, rewrite the observed event as a product of pairwise comparisons and smooth each one, as in @eq-dss-event. **Four.** State identification in terms of functions. Name the normalizations. Name the exclusion restriction, and be explicit that it is an assumption about the world. Then show which margin of the data identifies which object, as in the three lemmas of @sec-dss-identification. **Five.** Validate against a known truth before validating against a benchmark. The temperature pathology in @sec-dss-montecarlo is invisible in fit statistics and fatal to every estimate. A deep structural model has enough moving parts that a Monte Carlo where the truth lies inside the model class is not optional. **Six.** Report counterfactuals as the deliverable, and report the forecast alongside the choice. Picking the better of two policies is a weak test that a flexible predictor often passes. Forecasting what a policy will deliver, and answering about an intervention with no coefficient in the reduced form, is the test structure is for. ## Key Takeaways - Sequential search theory supplies a decision rule whose central object, the reservation utility of @weitzman1979optimal, is a monotone and differentiable function of the pre-search index and the search cost. That differentiability is what lets economics sit inside a neural network as an ordinary layer. - The SST of @song2026sst puts a transformer in the one slot where the classical search model was guessing: the map from a consumer's cross-session history to the utility they expect before clicking. Setting the deep components to zero recovers the classical model exactly, so the deep structure is a testable extension. - Identification in a deep structural model applies to functions. Under a scale and location normalization and the exclusion of slot position from utility, choice identifies the pre-search index, search order identifies differences in reservation cutoffs, and stopping identifies their level. The network weights are not identified and nothing of interest depends on them. - The differentiable likelihood requires smoothing a product of indicator functions. The smoothing temperature must be chosen jointly with the number of simulation draws. Too low a temperature produces a silent collapse of every coefficient toward zero, diagnosable without knowing the truth by checking whether the objective is stable as draws are added. - In our replication the deep components make the structural parameters estimable. The classical model mis-estimates the search-cost function because preference heterogeneity it cannot represent is absorbed into the search process. - Against a deep benchmark of equal capacity the structural model is ahead on prediction, by a wide margin on search depth and by a thin and sample-sensitive margin on purchase. Its decisive advantage lies elsewhere. Choosing between layouts is something a flexible predictor does just as well, because it needs only the ordering of preferences. Forecasting what a layout will earn, and answering about an intervention that has no coefficient in the reduced form at all, is what the structural half of the model is for.
